In its Old Testament uses, it functions as a descriptive word for the shape of sacred furnishings and other measured structures. The word can describe physical decay and serves as a picture of something weakened or corrupted. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Its noun function makes it the name of the authority or realm being discussed.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “place.” It functions as a relational word, identifying where one thing is in relation to another. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is used broadly, appearing 511 times across 450 verses, from Genesis through Malachi. Its role is often determined by the surrounding words and sentence, since it connects people, things, or actions with a place. The word also appears in passages describing God’s blessing and spoken declarations, where location is part of the relationship being expressed.

d: oppression

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to oppression—harmful treatment that weighs down or exploits people. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Psalms, so its normal sense is focused rather than broad. The English rendering is especially consistent with “oppression,” while related renderings also point toward deceit or fraud in two passages. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

d: power

e.t: This Hebrew word means “strength,” identifying the quality or condition of being strong. It functions as a term identifying strength rather than an action or a person’s name. Within the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs twice, both in Daniel: Daniel 2:37 and Daniel 4:30. In Daniel 2:37, the English rendering is “strength.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence.
